source.author: hor
source.text: non fumum ex fulgore, sed ex fumo dare lucem cogitat, ut speciosa dehinc miracula promat, Antiphaten, Scyllamque, et cum Cyclope Charybdim; nec reditum Diomedis ab interitu Meleagri nec gemino bellum Troianum orditur ab ovo: semper ad eventum festinat et in medias res non secus ac notas auditorem rapit et quae desperat tractata nitescere posse relinquit atque ita mentitur, sic veris falsa remiscet, primo ne medium, medio ne discrepet imum.
source.text_original: non fumum ex fulgore, sed ex fumo dare lucem  / cogitat, ut speciosa dehinc miracula promat,  / Antiphaten, Scyllamque, et cum Cyclope Charybdim;  / nec reditum Diomedis ab interitu Meleagri  / nec gemino bellum Troianum orditur ab ovo:  / semper ad eventum festinat et in medias res  / non secus ac notas auditorem rapit et quae  / desperat tractata nitescere posse relinquit  / atque ita mentitur, sic veris falsa remiscet,  / primo ne medium, medio ne discrepet imum.
source.text_english: he does not think to produce smoke from light, but light from smoke, so that thereafter he may unfold splendid marvels: Antiphates, and Scylla, and with the Cyclops Charybdis; nor does he begin the return of Diomedes from the death of Meleager, nor the Trojan War from the twin egg. He always hastens to the outcome and snatches the listener into the midst of things no differently than if they were familiar, and he leaves out what he despairs of making shine when handled; and so he invents, so he mingles falsehoods with truths, so that the middle may not be at variance with the beginning, nor the end with the middle.

reuse.author: hier
reuse.text: Quorsum, ais, ista tam alto repetita principio et ita procul coepta, ut merito quiuis Horatiano de nobis possit sale ludere: et gemino bellum Troianum orditur ab ouo? uidelicet ut senectutem tuam et caput ad Christi similitudinem candidum dignis uocibus praedicem.
reuse.text_original: 'Quorsum', ais, 'ista tam alto repetita principio et ita procul coepta, ut merito quiuis Horatiano de nobis possit sale ludere: et gemino bellum Troianum orditur ab ouo?' uidelicet ut senectutem tuam et caput ad Christi similitudinem candidum dignis uocibus praedicem.
reuse.text_english: To what end, you say, is this matter so far fetched from an exalted beginning and begun so far back that anyone could rightly mock us with Horace’s wit: and does he begin the Trojan War from the twin egg? Clearly, so that I may extol your old age and your head, white in the likeness of Christ, with fitting words.
